sections.title: Formulae, equations and calculations — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
The book opens this chapter with one of the biggest numbers you will meet
in chemistry: a single gold bar the size of the one in Figure 5.1 contains
almost **4 × 10²⁵ gold atoms** — that is 4 followed by 25 noughts. Counting
atoms one by one is obviously hopeless, so chemistry needs a way of
counting particles *by weighing*. That is what this chapter builds: the
**[[mole]]**, the unit chemists use for amount of substance, and the
calculations that flow from it — formulae, balanced equations, reacting
masses and yields.

:::prior-knowledge
You will use ideas from earlier chapters throughout: **balancing and
reading formulae** builds on writing word and symbol equations (Chapter 1);
the **relative atomic mass** recap in this chapter leans directly on
isotopes and weighted averages from Chapter 3 (page 26); and the
**Periodic Table** supplies the Aᵣ values you will be given in every
calculation.
:::

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- write **word equations** and **balanced chemical equations**, including
  **state symbols**, for familiar and unfamiliar reactions;
- calculate **relative formula masses (Mᵣ)** from relative atomic masses
  (Aᵣ), including for hydrated crystals such as CuSO₄·5H₂O;
- interconvert **masses in grams** and **amounts in moles**, and use the
  **[[avogadro-constant]]**;
- determine **empirical and molecular formulae** from experimental data —
  including by combustion and reduction of metal oxides, and water of
  crystallisation experiments;
- calculate **reacting masses** from chemical equations, decide which
  reagent is **in excess**, and calculate **percentage yields**.

:::exam-hint
The chapter's own objectives list is your revision checklist: every one of
its bullets is an examinable skill. Notice what the book chooses to
emphasise in its first objective — you must be able to write balanced
equations **including state symbols** both for reactions you have studied
*and* for unfamiliar reactions where you are given suitable information.
The unfamiliar-reaction half is where marks are commonly lost.
:::

:::misconception
"It says moles — so this chapter is about small furry animals burrowing
in the soil." The [[mole]] is a *counting unit*, like "a dozen" but for
6 × 10²³ particles. Nothing about it is furry; everything about it is
arithmetic. Chapter 3 gave you a taste of huge numbers (6 × 10²³ atoms in
the sports-hall thought experiment); this chapter turns that number into
a working tool.
:::

sections.title: Writing equations — word equations and symbol equations
sections.markdown:
The book draws a sharp line between the two types of chemical equation you
could be asked to write. A **[[word-equation]]** names the substances: for
example, *magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide*. A **[[chemical-equation]]**
(usually called a **symbol equation**) uses formulae instead:
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Symbol equations are what chemists normally use — the
book's instruction is that you should only write a word equation **if you
are specifically asked to**.

One rule sits above everything else in this section, and it applies to
both types: **all chemical equations must be balanced**. An unbalanced
equation is not a slightly imperfect answer — it is a wrong answer, because
it asserts that atoms can appear or disappear. The next four sections
build the balancing skill step by step, and the exam-hint below flags the
single most common way candidates throw marks away.

:::exam-hint
Read the book's instruction precisely: *you should only write a word
equation if you are specifically asked to*. If a question says "write an
equation", the examiner wants the **symbol** equation — a word equation
where a formula equation was expected scores little or nothing, even if
the chemistry is right.
:::

:::misconception
"A word equation and a symbol equation are two different reactions." No —
they are two *descriptions* of the same reaction. Mg + O₂ → 2MgO and
*magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide* carry exactly the same chemical
information; the symbol version additionally carries the proportions,
which is why it can (and must) be balanced.
:::

sections.title: What all the numbers in a formula mean
sections.markdown:
Before you can balance anything, you must be able to *count atoms through
a formula* — and that means understanding the two very different kinds of
number that appear in equations. The book uses the balanced equation

CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O

to make the point. A **big number written in front of a formula** (the
2 in 2HCl) is sometimes called a **[[coefficient]]**; it multiplies
*everything* in the formula. A **small subscript number** (the 3 in
CaCO₃) applies **only to the atom immediately before it**.

The book's second example, 2Cl → Cl₂, shows why the distinction matters
chemically, not just arithmetically: **2Cl** means two *separate* chlorine
atoms, while **Cl₂** means two chlorine atoms *joined in a molecule*. Same
atoms, completely different substances.

Work through the book's counting example: in **2H₂SO₄** the big 2 gives
you 2 molecules of sulfuric acid; each molecule has 2 hydrogens, 1 sulfur
and 4 oxygens. Count the atoms in the whole expression and you find
**4 hydrogens, 2 sulfurs and 8 oxygens**. Brackets extend the subscript's
reach: in **Ca(OH)₂** the 2 applies to *everything inside the bracket* —
1 calcium, 2 oxygens, 2 hydrogens. (The book points you to Chapter 7 for
how formulae like this are worked out.)

:::key-point
A small subscript number applies only to the atom immediately before it
in the formula. A subscript after brackets applies to everything inside
the brackets. A big number in front applies to the whole formula.
:::

:::exam-hint
Counting atoms through formulae with brackets is exactly where marks go
missing under time pressure. Practise until 2H₂SO₄ → 4 H, 2 S, 8 O and
Ca(OH)₂ → 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H are instant, because every balancing question
in this chapter — and every reacting-mass calculation later — stands on
this counting skill.
:::

:::misconception
"The 2 in 2H₂SO₄ means 2 sulfur atoms." It means **2 whole molecules** of
H₂SO₄ — so 2 sulfurs, 4 hydrogens, 8 oxygens in total. The big number
multiplies everything; the subscripts describe each single molecule.
Confusing the two scales of "two" is the root of most miscounts.
:::

sections.title: Balancing equations
sections.markdown:
Chemical reactions **rearrange atoms into new combinations** — they never
create or destroy them. It follows that a finished equation must end up
with exactly the same number of each type of atom that it started with;
that is what makes it a **[[balanced-equation]]**. The book builds the
idea with methane burning in oxygen:

CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

Count the atoms on each side and the equation *can't* be right: the right
side has gained an oxygen atom and lost two hydrogens. The substances are
all correct — methane really does burn to carbon dioxide and water — so,
as the book puts it, **the proportions must be wrong**. Fixing
proportions, without touching the substances, is the whole skill.

The book's HINT on page 40 is the single most important sentence in this
chapter, and it deserves to be quoted in full: you must **never, never
change a formula** when balancing an equation. All you are allowed to do
is write **big numbers in front of the formulae**. The next section
applies the fix to the methane equation, and Worked example 1 shows the
systematic method in action.

:::exam-hint
This HINT is really important (the book's own emphasis): **never change a
formula when balancing**. If the equation needs another oxygen, you write
a bigger *big number* — you never turn O₂ into O₃ or H₂O into H₂O₂.
Changing a formula changes the substances, which changes the chemistry;
changing a big number changes only the proportions, which is what
balancing means.
:::

:::misconception
"CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O is nearly balanced, so it is nearly right." There is
no such thing as *nearly* balanced — an equation either conserves every
atom type or it is wrong. Here the left side has 4 H and 2 O while the
right has 2 H and 3 O. The chemistry (which substances) is fine; the
proportions (how much of each) are not, and only the proportions may be
edited.
:::

sections.title: Try again — balancing the methane equation
sections.markdown:
The book now fixes the methane equation. With the proportions adjusted —
and *only* the proportions — the balanced equation for the combustion of
methane is:

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

Count each symbol as one atom of that element and check both sides:
**1 carbon** each side; **4 hydrogens** each side (4 on the left inside
CH₄, 2 × 2 on the right inside 2H₂O); **4 oxygens** each side (2 × 2 on
the left, 2 + 2 on the right). Every atom type balances — this is what
the book calls *balancing the equation*.

Balancing is a skill with a method, and the book gives you its systematic
approach directly. Follow it exactly as printed:

- **Work across the equation from left to right**, checking one element
  after another. If an element seems impossible to fix that way, leave it
  until the end — you will often find it has sorted itself out.
- **Count unchanged groups as a whole.** If a group of atoms such as the
  sulfate group (SO₄) appears unchanged on both sides, count the group
  once instead of individual sulfurs and oxygens. It saves time.
- **Check everything at the end**, to be sure you have not disturbed
  something you already counted.

:::exam-hint
The book's three-step method is worth adopting verbatim: left-to-right,
one element at a time; unchanged atom-groups counted whole; full recount
at the end. The "leave the awkward element until last" tip is the one
that rescues equations involving O₂ — you will see exactly why in
Worked example 2 (the ethane combustion).
:::

:::misconception
"I balanced it left to right, so it must still be balanced when I finish."
Not necessarily — fixing a later element can *unbalance* an earlier one
(for instance, changing 2H₂O on the right alters both the H and the O
counts). That is precisely why the book's method ends with **check
everything at the end**: the last pass is not optional tidying, it is
where the marks are secured.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 1 — balancing zinc + hydrochloric acid
sections.markdown:
Balance the equation for the reaction between zinc and hydrochloric acid:

Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂

The book works the systematic method from the previous section, left to
right. **Zinc**: 1 atom on each side — no problem. **Hydrogen**: 1 atom on
the left, 2 on the right; if there are 2 at the end, there must have been
2 at the start, and the only way to achieve that is **2HCl**. (You must
*not* change the formula to H₂Cl, because that substance does not exist.)
**Chlorine**: with 2HCl there are now 2 on each side — good. Finally
check everything again, and the equation is finished:

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂

The book's atom-count table for the finished equation:

|                | Zn | H | Cl | Zn | H | Cl |
|----------------|----|---|----|----|---|----|
| numbers of atoms | 1 | 2 | 2  | 1 | 2 | 2  |

:::key-point
Halves *are* acceptable in balanced equations, and you can always remove
one later by doubling everything — but you will rarely meet them at
International GCSE. Worked example 2 shows the halving trick in its
natural habitat: an odd number of oxygens.
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's second HINT in this section settles two state-symbol worries
before they start: don't worry if you don't yet know what the state
symbols should be — that is not important at this stage. But do register
the correction it adds: **water is a liquid (l), not an aqueous solution
(aq)** — an aqueous solution is formed when something is *dissolved in*
water.
:::

:::misconception
"If I need 2 hydrogens on the left, I can write H₂Cl." You cannot —
**H₂Cl is not a substance**. Hydrochloric acid is HCl, period. Balancing
adjusts *how many* formula units take part (the big number 2HCl); it
never rewrites *what* the substance is. This is the never-change-a-formula
law from the last section, caught red-handed in exam conditions.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 2 — balancing the combustion of ethane
sections.markdown:
Balance the equation for the combustion of ethane:

C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

The book's systematic method, left to right. **Carbons**: 2 on the left,
so 2CO₂ on the right. **Hydrogens**: 6 on the left, so 3H₂O on the right.
**Oxygens**: now there are 7 on the right ((2 × 2) + 3) but only 2 on the
left — and here comes the problem the book wants you to recognise: oxygen
atoms have to travel **in pairs** (O₂ molecules), so you cannot put an
odd number like 7 of them on the left directly.

The trick: **allow yourself halves**. 7 oxygen atoms is the same as
3½ oxygen molecules:

C₂H₆ + 3½O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

Then **double everything** to remove the fraction:

2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O

:::key-point
Halving (then doubling the whole equation) is the standard escape from an
odd number of oxygens. You might reasonably object that half an O₂
molecule is not a physical thing — the doubling step answers that
objection; the final equation has only whole numbers.
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's KEY POINT in this section adds the full context: halves are
*acceptable* in balanced equations, but you will rarely meet them at
International GCSE — and if you do produce one, **double everything**
rather than leaving it. An examiner will accept either the halved or the
doubled form; the doubled form is the one you should hand in.
:::

:::misconception
"I can't balance this — 7 oxygens can't come from O₂ molecules, so the
reaction must be wrong." The reaction is fine; your *temporary* arithmetic
is what needs the half. Oxygen atoms still conserve: 14 on the left
(7 O₂ × 2), 14 on the right (4 CO₂ gives 8 + 6 H₂O gives 6). The half
molecule is scaffolding, removed by the doubling step before you write
your final answer.
:::

:::

sections.title: State symbols
sections.markdown:
**State symbols** are often — but not always — written after each formula
in an equation to show the **physical state** everything is in. The book
gives you the four you need to know:

| Symbol | State |
|--------|-------|
| (s) | solid |
| (l) | liquid |
| (g) | gas |
| (aq) | in aqueous solution (dissolved in water) |

The book's worked illustration:

2K(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2KOH(aq) + H₂(g)

Read aloud, this says: solid potassium reacts with liquid water to make a
solution of potassium hydroxide in water, and hydrogen gas. Notice how
much extra information the state symbols carry — the same balanced
equation *without* them would not tell you that the potassium hydroxide
ends up dissolved, or that the hydrogen leaves as a gas.

:::exam-hint
The two symbols candidates mix up are **(l)** and **(aq)**. Water in a
beaker is H₂O(**l**); salt *dissolved in* that water is NaCl(**aq**). The
book's own HINT from the previous section said it plainly: water is a
liquid, not an aqueous solution — (aq) is reserved for something
dissolved in water. State symbols are part of the 1.25 objective
("including state symbols"), so a perfectly balanced equation can still
drop marks without them.
:::

:::misconception
"(aq) means 'in water', so pure water is H₂O(aq)." No — (aq) means
*dissolved in water*, which requires something doing the dissolving.
Pure water is the solvent itself: H₂O(**l**). Only species dissolved in
water — ions like KOH(aq) above — earn the (aq) label.
:::

sections.title: How much of each substance reacts? — the carbon-12 scale and Aᵣ
sections.markdown:
The book sets up the whole second half of the chapter with a practical
question: make iron(II) sulfide by heating iron with sulfur —

Fe + S → FeS

— and ask: **in what proportions should you mix them?** Certainly not
equal masses, because iron and sulfur atoms do not weigh the same. An
iron atom contains more protons and neutrons than a sulfur atom, so it is
about **one and three-quarter times heavier**. Getting the proportions
right therefore requires knowing the masses of the individual atoms
taking part — which is exactly what the **[[relative-atomic-mass]]**
delivers.

**The carbon-12 scale.** A single atom weighs about
1.67 × 10⁻²⁴ g — an absurd number to calculate with. Instead, chemists
compare all atomic masses against a standard: the mass of an atom of the
**carbon-12 isotope** ([[carbon-12-scale]]). On this scale one ¹²C atom
weighs **exactly 12 units**, and the basic unit of the scale is
**one-twelfth** of that — approximately the mass of the most common
hydrogen atom. So fluorine-19 has a relative mass of **19** (19 times
one-twelfth of a ¹²C atom), and magnesium's most common isotope has a
relative mass of **24**.

**From isotopes to Aᵣ.** Real samples contain a *mixture* of isotopes, so
we need the average mass of an atom taking them all into account — the
relative atomic mass. The book's definition, verbatim:

> The relative atomic mass of an element is the **weighted average mass**
> of the isotopes of the element. It is measured on **the carbon-12
> scale**, on which a carbon-12 (¹²C) atom has a mass of **exactly 12**.

Because these are *relative* masses, they have **no units**. Chlorine's
Aᵣ is 35.45 (quoted 35.5), lithium's is 6.94 (quoted 7), sodium's is
22.99 (quoted 23) — averages over their isotope mixtures. The book's
convention for International GCSE: use the Periodic Table values, with
decimals where given (Cl 35.5, Cu 63.5).

:::key-point
To work out a weighted average you have to know **how much of each isotope
is present** in the sample — the weighted-average method from Chapter 3
(page 26) is the same mathematics again here.
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's HINT draws a vocabulary line the examiner enforces: avoid
**'relative molecular mass'** for ionic substances — it can only properly
describe actual molecules (covalent substances). You should not use it
for magnesium oxide or sodium chloride. **Relative formula mass covers
everything**, which is why the next section installs it as the default
term.
:::

:::misconception
"Aᵣ = 35.5 means a chlorine atom weighs 35.5 units." No single chlorine
atom does — 35.5 is the **weighted average** across the ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl
mixture. Any one atom weighs 35 or 37; the *sample average* is 35.5.
This is the Chapter 3 isotope story (weighted averages need how much of
each isotope is present) reappearing as the foundation for Mᵣ.
:::

sections.title: Relative formula mass (Mᵣ)
sections.markdown:
Compounds get weighed on the same carbon-12 scale as atoms. A water
molecule, H₂O, has a mass of **18** on this scale — 18 times the mass of
one-twelfth of a ¹²C atom. For compounds the term is
**[[relative-formula-mass]]**, given the symbol **Mᵣ** (the book notes it
is sometimes called [[relative-molecular-mass]] — the previous section's
HINT explains why *formula* mass is the safer phrase: it covers ionic
substances too).

Calculating an Mᵣ is bookkeeping: **add up the relative atomic masses of
every atom in the formula**, using the Periodic Table. The book's
copper(II) sulfate crystals example, CuSO₄·5H₂O, shows the one twist you
must be ready for. When some substances crystallise from solution, water
becomes **chemically bound** to the salt — [[water-of-crystallisation]] —
and the bound water is *part of the formula*: there are always 5 water
molecules per CuSO₄ unit, and salts carrying it are **hydrated**. (Other
examples the book lists: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O and MgCl₂·6H₂O.)

:::key-point
Relative atomic masses are **always given** in the exam — in the question
or on the Periodic Table. You never calculate Aᵣ yourself; but if you use
the Periodic Table, take the **larger of the two numbers** (the relative
atomic mass, not the atomic number).
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's HINT on hydrated formulae flags the classic miscount: work out
the hydrogens and oxygens of the water **as complete H₂O units**, not
separately. The common mistake is to get 10 hydrogens right (2 × 5) but
then count only **1** oxygen instead of **5**. Five waters = 10 H **and**
5 O. (The book's Figure 5.8 shows the structure: five water molecules
bonded to each copper(II) sulfate unit — and it writes copper(II)
properly: capital I twice, not Il.)
:::

:::misconception
"The ·5H₂O in CuSO₄·5H₂O is just wet salt — you can ignore it in
calculations." You cannot. The water of crystallisation is **chemically
bound** and part of the formula; the salt is *hydrated*, and its Mᵣ
includes all five waters. Ignoring them turns every downstream
percentage-composition and mole calculation on this salt into a wrong
answer.
:::

sections.title: Using relative formula mass to find percentage composition
sections.markdown:
Once you have an Mᵣ, one division tells you what fraction of a compound's
mass any part of it contributes — the **[[percentage-composition]]**. The
book's first worked case, magnesium carbonate:

**To find the Mᵣ of MgCO₃** (Aᵣ values: C = 12, O = 16, Mg = 24):

Mᵣ = 24 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 24 + 12 + 48 = **84**

You add the masses of 1 × Mg, 1 × C and 3 × O — the subscripts do the
counting. The second case adds brackets to the arithmetic, calcium
hydroxide:

**To find the Mᵣ of Ca(OH)₂** (Aᵣ values: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1):

Mᵣ = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = **74**

The bracketed (OH) group is counted **as a unit** (16 + 1 = 17) and then
doubled — exactly the bracket rule from section 3, now earning its keep
in a calculation. With the Mᵣ in hand, the percentage by mass of any
element follows: that element's total contribution divided by the whole,
× 100. The next two sections work that division through two complete
examples.

:::exam-hint
Two habits from the book's presentation are worth copying in the exam.
First, **write the Aᵣ values down before starting** — the book always
lists them ("Relative atomic masses: C = 12, O = 16, Mg = 24") even
though they are given, because it makes the working checkable. Second,
multiply first, add second: 3 × 16 = 48 as its own step stops the
"C + O₃" addition errors.
:::

:::misconception
"Mᵣ of Ca(OH)₂ is 40 + 16 + 1 + 2 = 59." The 2 after the bracket doubles
**everything inside it** — both the O and the H. Correct working is
40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74. Forgetting to multiply the hydrogen is
the bracket-rule failure wearing a calculation costume.
:::

sections.title: Worked example — Mᵣ of copper(II) sulfate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O
sections.markdown:
This formula looks far more complicated than the previous ones — and the
book's advice is to break it into its two natural pieces. First, why the
water is there at all: when some substances crystallise from solution,
water becomes **chemically bound up with the salt**. This is
[[water-of-crystallisation]], and salts containing it are **hydrated**
([[hydrated-salt]]). There are **always 5 water molecules per 1 CuSO₄
unit** — they are part of the formula, not impurities. (The book's other
examples: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O and MgCl₂·6H₂O.)

**To find the Mᵣ of CuSO₄·5H₂O** (Aᵣ values: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32,
Cu = 63.5).

The book's method: work out the relative formula mass of water first, then
add the correct number of waters on to the rest of the formula:

- **Water**: Mᵣ(H₂O) = (2 × 1) + 16 = **18**
- **The salt part**: Mᵣ(CuSO₄) = 63.5 + 32 + (4 × 16) = 63.5 + 32 + 64 = **159.5**
- **Assemble**: 159.5 + (5 × 18) = 159.5 + 90 = **249.5**

The same section then points the tool at a single element — **to find the
percentage by mass of copper in copper(II) oxide, CuO** (Aᵣ: O = 16,
Cu = 63.5): Mᵣ(CuO) = 63.5 + 16 = 79.5, of which **63.5 is copper**, so
the copper percentage is (63.5 / 79.5) × 100 ≈ **79.9%**. "Having found
the relative formula mass of a compound, we can work out the percentage
by mass of any part of it" — the book's own bridge to the next section.

:::key-point
For a hydrated salt, compute the water's Mᵣ once (18 for H₂O) and multiply
by the number of waters of crystallisation. The dot · in the formula
means "plus this many whole waters per formula unit" — nothing more
mysterious than that.
:::

:::exam-hint
Structure your Mᵣ working for hydrated salts exactly as the book does:
salt part, water part, assemble. Examiners award method marks for the
stages — a bare "249.5" with no visible 159.5 + 90 can lose the working
mark even with the right answer. And quote Mᵣ(CuSO₄·5H₂O) = 249.5 —
this exact value returns in Worked example 7 (percentage yield of these
very crystals).
:::

:::misconception
"CuSO₄·5H₂O means CuSO₄ joined to 5 separate H₂O molecules floating

crystal structure — the book's Figure 5.8 shows them bonded to each
CuSO₄ unit. They are not loose water you could shake off; heating is
needed to drive them out (that experiment is Worked example 6's
neighbour, section 26).

sections.title: Worked example — percentage by mass of oxygen in sodium carbonate
sections.markdown:
**To find the percentage by mass of oxygen in sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃**
(Aᵣ values: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16).

The book's Figure 5.9 sits beside this calculation for a reason: it shows
1-mole quantities of carbon (12 g), sulfur (32 g), iron (56 g), copper
(63.5 g) and magnesium (24 g) — the bridge from formula-mass arithmetic to
the mole, which the very next section makes explicit. Here, the
calculation runs:

1. **Mᵣ(Na₂CO₃)** = (2 × 23) + 12 + (3 × 16) = 46 + 12 + 48 = **106**
2. **Oxygen's contribution**: there are 3 oxygens in the formula, so the
   total mass of oxygen is 3 × 16 = **48**
3. **Percentage**: (48 / 106) × 100 ≈ **45.3%**

The book underlines step 2 in words: "48 of this 106 is due to the oxygen
(remember that there are 3 oxygens in the formula, so the total mass of
oxygen is 3 × 16 = 48)." The multiply-before-you-divide structure is the
whole method: count the element's atoms, total their mass, divide by the
compound's Mᵣ.

:::exam-hint
Carry the "total mass of the element" as its own named step (3 × 16 = 48)
before dividing by 106. This is exactly the book's presentation, and it
is also self-checking: the three element percentages (Na, C, O) must sum
to 100% — a quick sanity check that catches subscript slips on the spot.
:::

:::misconception
"Oxygen is 16/106 ≈ 15% of the compound." That divides *one* oxygen's mass
by the whole. The formula has **three** oxygens: 48/106 ≈ 45.3%. The
subscript is part of the mass arithmetic, not decoration — every atom in
the formula contributes its Aᵣ to the element's share.
:::

sections.title: The mole
sections.markdown:
In chemistry, the **[[mole]]** is a unit of the **amount of substance**.
You can express an amount in grams *or* in moles — and the difference
between the two expressions is that **1 mole of any substance has its own
particular mass**. The book's examples: 1 mole of water has a mass of
18 g, 1 mole of sulfur 32 g, 1 mole of magnesium oxide 40 g. The
abbreviation for mole is **mol**.

So the same sample can be described both ways: 36 g of water **is** 2 mol
(because 1 mol of water is 18 g); but 36 g of sulfur is only 1.125 mol
(1 mol of sulfur is 32 g), and 36 g of magnesium is 1.5 mol (1 mol of
magnesium is 24 g). Same 36 grams — different amounts of substance,
because the particles weigh different amounts. The book also settles the
phrasing: "amount in moles" and "number of moles" mean the same thing,
just as "amount in grams" and "number of grams" do.

**Where the mass of 1 mole comes from**: calculate the relative formula
mass (Mᵣ) and **attach the units, grams**. The book works three:

- **1 mole of oxygen gas, O₂** (Aᵣ: O = 16): Mᵣ = 32, so 1 mol has a mass
  of **32 g**.
- **1 mole of calcium chloride, CaCl₂** (Aᵣ: Cl = 35.5, Ca = 40):
  Mᵣ = 40 + (2 × 35.5) = 111, so 1 mol has a mass of **111 g**.
- **1 mole of iron(II) sulfate crystals, FeSO₄·7H₂O** (Aᵣ: H = 1, O = 16,
  S = 32, Fe = 56): Mᵣ = 56 + 32 + (4 × 16) + 7 × [(2 × 1) + 16] =
  56 + 32 + 64 + 126 = **278**, so 1 mol has a mass of **278 g** — the
  hydrated-crystal method from section 12, reused without ceremony.

:::key-point
Mass of 1 mole = Mᵣ expressed in grams. This is the [[molar-mass]] idea —
the book's next section adds the terminology and its one fine-print
distinction.
:::

:::exam-hint
Notice the oxygen example specifies **oxygen gas, O₂** — 32 g, not 16 g.
Whenever a question says "1 mole of oxygen", check whether it means atoms
(O, 16 g) or molecules (O₂, 32 g): the next section makes quoting the
formula compulsory for exactly this reason.
:::

:::misconception
"1 mole of every substance weighs the same." That is the property of 1
*mole* (it contains the same *number* of particles — section 17) — not of
1 mole's *mass*. 1 mol of water is 18 g, 1 mol of sulfur 32 g, 1 mol of
MgO 40 g: equal particle counts, unequal masses, because their particles
are differently heavy.
:::

sections.title: Quoting the formula — and the molar mass vocabulary
sections.markdown:
Whenever you talk about a mole of something, **you must quote its
formula** — otherwise there is a real risk of confusion. The book's
example is the classic: "1 mole of oxygen" could mean

- 1 mole of oxygen **atoms**, O, with a mass of **16 g**, or
- 1 mole of oxygen **molecules**, O₂, with a mass of **32 g**.

Twice the mass, same words. The formula is what disambiguates, which is
why exam answers (and the book itself) never say "oxygen" without the
formula when a mole calculation is in play.

The book's HINTS in this section assemble the vocabulary and the number
sense you need:

- **'Molar mass' is often used instead of 'mass of 1 mole'** — same
  practical meaning at this level.
- Fine print (book's EXTENSION WORK, for completeness): strictly, molar
  mass has units of **g/mol** while mass of 1 mole has units of **g**.
  You are unlikely to need the distinction at International GCSE.
- **Don't over-rely on learned formulae**: if 1 mole weighs 100 g, it
  should be obvious that 2 moles weigh twice as much, 10 moles ten times
  as much, 0.2 moles 0.2 times as much.
- **Division as sense-check**: if 1 mol weighs 18 g, the number of moles
  in 54 g is simply *how many times 18 goes into 54*. If you feel safer
  with a formula, use it — but never let the formula replace the sanity
  check.

:::exam-hint
The "how many times does it go in?" instinct is a genuine exam tool: in
54 g of water, 18 goes in 3 times → 3 mol. Do this mental division
*before* reaching for moles = mass/Mᵣ, and you will catch flipped
fractions (Mᵣ/mass) before they cost you the answer — 18/54 would
plainly be nonsense here.
:::

:::misconception
"'Moles of oxygen' is a complete answer." It is not — the examiner cannot
mark what they cannot interpret. "1 mol oxygen" is ambiguous between
16 g (atoms) and 32 g (molecules); always write **1 mol O₂** or
**1 mol O**. The book's rule: quote the formula, every time.
:::

sections.title: Simple calculations with moles
sections.markdown:
You need to be able to **interconvert between a mass in grams and an
amount in moles** for a given substance. There is one formula to learn:

$$\text{number of moles} = \frac{\text{mass (g)}}{\text{mass of 1 mole (g)}}$$

You can rearrange it to find whatever you want. If rearranging causes
problems, the book offers a **triangular arrangement** (Figure 5.10):
mass on top, number of moles and mass of 1 mole on the bottom — cover the
quantity you want and the triangle shows the operation (top ÷ bottom, or
bottom × bottom, or top ÷ bottom). Look at it carefully, the book says,
and make sure you can deduce all three equations from it.

The book's two worked cases, both with the Mᵣ found first:

**Finding the mass of 0.2 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃**
(Aᵣ: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40):

- Mᵣ(CaCO₃) = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = **100**, so 1 mol has a mass of 100 g
- 0.2 mol has a mass of 0.2 × 100 = **20 g**

**Finding the number of moles in 54 g of water, H₂O**
(Aᵣ: H = 1, O = 16):

- Mᵣ(H₂O) = (2 × 1) + 16 = **18**, so 1 mol has a mass of 18 g
- 54 g of water is 54 / 18 = **3 mol**

:::key-point
Number of moles = mass in grams ÷ mass of 1 mole in grams. Every
remaining calculation in this chapter — reacting masses, yields, excess —
is this line plus a chemical equation.
:::

:::exam-hint
Always find (and *show*) the Mᵣ first, exactly as the book does. The two
workings above each carry three visible stages — Mᵣ, then the mole-mass
link, then the answer. That structure earns method marks even when an
arithmetic slip lands late, and it makes your answer checkable by the
"how many times does it go in?" instinct from the last section.
:::

:::misconception
"moles = mass ÷ Mᵣ, so to get the mass I also divide by Mᵣ." Rearrange,
don't repeat: **mass = moles × mass of 1 mole**. The two directions are
the triangle's two different reads — 0.2 mol × 100 g/mol = 20 g versus
54 g ÷ 18 g/mol = 3 mol. Writing the division both ways is the single
most common mole-arithmetic slip.
:::

sections.title: Moles and the Avogadro constant
sections.markdown:
Here is the number that makes the mole worth having. Imagine 1 mole of
¹²C: it has a mass of **12 g** and contains about **6 × 10²³ carbon
atoms** — 6 followed by 23 noughts. That number of particles in 12 g of
¹²C is the **[[avogadro-constant]]**.

And the punchline: **1 mole of anything else contains this same number of
particles**. The book's examples:

- 1 mole of magnesium contains 6 × 10²³ magnesium atoms, Mg, and has a
  mass of **24 g**
- 1 mole of water contains 6 × 10²³ water molecules, H₂O, and has a mass
  of **18 g**

This is *the reason we use moles*, in the book's own words: **if we know
the number of moles we also know how many particles are present** — and
if we know how many particles are present, we can work out how much of
one substance reacts with a certain amount of another. Reactions happen
particle-by-particle; the mole is the bridge from the grams you can weigh
to the particles that actually react.

The book's Figure 5.11 scale check: approximately 1 × 10³² water
molecules go over Niagara Falls *every second* in summer — 100 million
million million million million molecules. Against that, 6 × 10²³ is a
small, weighable, laboratory-sized crowd.

:::key-point
Equal moles = equal numbers of particles, regardless of substance. 1 mol
of Mg and 1 mol of H₂O both carry 6 × 10²³ particles — the masses differ
(24 g vs 18 g) because the particles differ; the *counts* do not.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two forms of the same fact get tested: the Avogadro constant value
(**6 × 10²³ per mole**) and the inference (*moles → particles*: 0.5 mol
of Mg contains 0.5 × 6 × 10²³ = 3 × 10²³ atoms). Watch the book's own
precision habit in its examples — "about 6 × 10²³", "approximately" —
the constant is quoted to one significant figure at this level.
:::

:::misconception
"1 mole of magnesium has more particles than 1 mole of water, because
magnesium atoms are heavier." Heavier particles mean a **greater mass**
(24 g vs 18 g) — but the **count is identical**: 6 × 10²³ each. A mole
is a count, not a weight; that is precisely why it can convert between
the two.
:::

sections.title: Formulae — from mole ratios to empirical and molecular formulae
sections.markdown:
Formulae come *from* mole ratios. The book starts with sulfur dioxide,
SO₂: there are 2 O atoms for each S atom. Scale it up — if you had 1 mol
of SO₂ you would still have twice as many O atoms as S atoms: **1 mol of
S atoms and 2 mol of O atoms**. And back down: if an experiment found a
sample of sulfur dioxide containing 0.1 mol of S atoms, it must also
contain **0.2 mol of O atoms** (0.2 mol contains twice as many atoms as
0.1 mol — the book's KEY POINT makes the same point with 0.02 vs 0.01
mol).

Run the logic forward and you can *read formulae out of mole data*:

- A compound contains **0.2 mol Ca and 0.2 mol O** → equal numbers of
  atoms → the formula is **CaO**.
- A compound contains **0.4 mol Mn and 0.8 mol O** → twice as many O
  atoms as Mn atoms → the formula is **MnO₂**.

Formulae found this way have names, and the book defines both:

> The **[[empirical-formula]]** shows the **simplest whole number ratio**
> of the atoms present in a compound.
>
> The **[[molecular-formula]]** shows the **actual number of atoms of each
> element** present in a molecule (covalent compound) or formula unit
> (ionic compound) of a compound.

The two can coincide or differ: calcium oxide is CaO *both* ways; hydrogen
peroxide has empirical formula **HO** but molecular formula **H₂O₂**. To
get from one to the other you need one extra datum — the Mᵣ of the
compound — which is exactly the machinery the next four sections build.

:::key-point
Mole ratios *are* atom ratios. The empirical formula is that ratio in
simplest whole numbers; the molecular formula is the actual atom count,
and it is always the empirical formula (or a whole-number multiple of it).
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's HINT on this page is a significant-figures confession: more
significant figures *should* have been used for the numbers of moles in
these examples, but were omitted for simplicity. In the exam, carry more
figures through the intermediate mole values (the practicals later give
0.0400 vs 0.040 for exactly this reason) and only round at the ratio.
:::

:::misconception
"The empirical formula and molecular formula are always different." They
are often the same — CaO is both. They differ only when the molecular
formula is a *multiple* of the simplest ratio (HO vs H₂O₂). Treating
"empirical" as automatically "not the real formula" is wrong; treating it
as automatically "the real formula" is wrong too — you need the Mᵣ to
decide (section 23).
:::

sections.title: Worked examples 3 and 4 — empirical formulae from masses
sections.markdown:
In order to find the empirical formula of a compound such as copper oxide,
we need to know how many atoms of copper combine with how many atoms of
oxygen — and we work atoms out from **moles**. If we know the ratio
between the numbers of copper and oxygen atoms, we know the formula.

**Example 3** — a sample of a compound contains **1.27 g of Cu** and
**0.16 g of O**. Calculate the empirical formula (Aᵣ: Cu = 63.5, O = 16).
It is easiest in columns, using a table:

|                                             | Cu        | O         |
|---------------------------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| masses/g                                    | 1.27      | 0.16      |
| moles of atoms = mass ÷ mass of 1 mole of atoms | 1.27/63.5 | 0.16/16   |
| number of moles of atoms                    | 0.02      | 0.01      |
| divide by the **smaller** number for the ratio | 0.02/0.01 | 0.01/0.01 |
| ratio of moles                              | 2         | 1         |
| empirical formula                           | **Cu₂O**  |           |

There are twice as many moles of Cu as O — so twice as many Cu atoms as O
atoms in the compound. One warning from the book that examiners love:
we are counting **atoms**, so we divide by the mass of 1 mole of oxygen
**atoms** (16), **not** by 32 (the mass of 1 mole of oxygen *molecules*).

**Example 4** — a sample contains **0.78 g of K, 1.10 g of Mn and
1.28 g of O** (Aᵣ: K = 39, Mn = 55, O = 16). Again, a table:

|                                             | K       | Mn      | O        |
|---------------------------------------------|---------|---------|----------|
| masses/g                                    | 0.78    | 1.10    | 1.28     |
| moles of atoms = mass ÷ mass of 1 mole of atoms | 0.78/39 | 1.10/55 | 1.28/16  |
| number of moles of atoms                    | 0.02    | 0.02    | 0.08     |
| divide by the smallest number for the ratio | 0.02/0.02 | 0.02/0.02 | 0.08/0.02 |
| ratio of moles                              | 1       | 1       | 4        |
| empirical formula                           | **KMnO₄** |         |          |

:::exam-hint
The book's HINT on this page: the original masses were measured to
2 significant figures, so the numbers of moles should also be given to
2 significant figures (0.010). If you write 0.01 in the exam that is fine
and still gives the correct answer — but match your figure count to your
data, deliberately rather than accidentally.
:::

:::misconception
"0.16 g of O is 0.16/32 = 0.005 mol, so the formula would be Cu₄O." The
compound's formula counts **atoms**, and the oxygen in it arrived as
individual atoms — divide by 16 (1 mol of O atoms), not 32 (1 mol of O₂
molecules). The book stops mid-chapter to say exactly this; it is the
single most common empirical-formula slip.
:::

sections.title: Practicals — finding the formula of a metal oxide by combustion and by reduction
sections.markdown:
Spec 1.36 is a practical: **know how to determine the formula of a metal
oxide by combustion or by reduction**. The book gives both experiments,
each ending in the same empirical-formula table.

## By combustion — magnesium oxide (Figure 5.12)

Burn magnesium in oxygen and watch how the mass changes. Procedure:
weigh a crucible **with its lid**; add a ~10 cm piece of magnesium ribbon
and weigh again; heat strongly (a roaring flame), **lifting the lid every
few seconds**; cool and weigh when finished. The magnesium burns with a
bright white flame to give magnesium oxide, a white powder. The lid
stops the powder escaping — but it must be lifted to **let oxygen in**.

A set of results: crucible 32.46 g; + magnesium 32.70 g; + contents at
the end 32.86 g.

- mass of magnesium = 32.70 − 32.46 = **0.24 g**
- the mass **increases** because the magnesium combines with oxygen from
  the air: mass of oxygen gained = 32.86 − 32.70 = **0.16 g**
- the reaction type was **[[combustion]]**

The empirical-formula table (Aᵣ: Mg = 24, O = 16):

|                 | Mg        | O         |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------|
| masses/g        | 0.24      | 0.16      |
| moles of atoms  | 0.24/24   | 0.16/16   |
| number of moles | 0.010     | 0.010     |
| ÷ smaller       | 1         | 1         |
| empirical formula | **MgO** |           |

:::safety
Wear eye protection and take care not to get burned when raising the
crucible lid with tongs. The crucible will stay very hot for some time.
:::

## By reduction — copper oxide (Figure 5.13)

Alternatively, **remove the oxygen** and watch the mass fall. Pass
hydrogen gas over copper oxide in a ceramic dish inside a tube; ignite
the excess hydrogen at the small hole; heat strongly until pink-brown
copper is seen. Results: dish 23.78 g; + copper oxide 26.96 g; + contents
at end 26.32 g.

- mass of copper oxide = 26.96 − 23.78 = **3.18 g**
- mass of copper at the end = 26.32 − 23.78 = **2.54 g**
- mass of oxygen removed = 3.18 − 2.54 = **0.64 g**

The reaction, CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, is a **[[displacement-reaction]]**
(hydrogen is more reactive than copper and displaces it) — and can also
be called a **[[redox-reaction]]**: the copper oxide has been
**reduced** — oxygen removed, the [[reduction]] of the copper(II) oxide. Chapter 14 develops both.

The table (Aᵣ: Cu = 63.5, O = 16): 2.54/63.5 = 0.0400 mol Cu;
0.64/16 = 0.040 mol O; ratio 1 : 1 → empirical formula **CuO**.

:::safety
The teacher demonstrating needs to wear a face shield and use safety
screens; pupils require eye protection and should be no closer than
2 metres. If a drying agent is needed, use anhydrous calcium chloride —
NOT concentrated sulfuric acid.
:::

:::key-point
Before lighting the hydrogen stream, **fill the whole tube with
hydrogen first**: a hydrogen–oxygen mixture is explosive. Let the gas
flow through for a while to flush out all the oxygen, then light the
stream (or the Bunsen burner).
:::

:::key-point
How do you know the reaction has finished? Nothing more happens in the
crucible — and you check by **heating to constant mass**: weigh, heat,
weigh again, repeating until the mass stays constant. (The book's HINT:
the original masses here are 2 significant figures, so quote the moles
as 0.010 — the extra figure shows the precision honestly.)
:::

:::exam-hint
In practice the ratio "is not very often" exactly 1:1 — the book lists
the experimental culprits: some magnesium oxide powder may escape when
the lid is lifted; not all the magnesium may react; and magnesium can
also react with **nitrogen** in the air. Expect a question to hand you a
slightly-off ratio and ask which of these explains it — that question is
asking for this list.
:::

:::misconception
"The mass went down in the reduction experiment, so matter was
destroyed." The oxygen **left the dish as water vapour** — hydrogen
carried it away. Every gram is conserved: 0.64 g of oxygen moved from
copper oxide into the water stream. "Mass decrease" in this experiment
means *oxygen removed*, i.e. reduction — not loss of matter.
:::

sections.title: Determining the formula of water
sections.markdown:
Modify the reduction apparatus of Figure 5.13 slightly — Figure 5.14 —
and the same experiment determines **the formula of water**: this time
the **water vapour** produced by the reaction between copper(II) oxide
and hydrogen is **condensed** in a U-tube and collected. The dish is
weighed before and after as before, **and** the mass of water collected
is measured.

The results table adds one row to the reduction experiment's:

|                                        | g      |
|----------------------------------------|--------|
| mass of empty dish                     | 23.78  |
| mass of dish + copper oxide            | 26.96  |
| mass of dish + contents at end         | 26.32  |
| mass of water collected                | **0.72** |

The reasoning, in the book's steps: the mass of oxygen lost from the
copper(II) oxide is **0.64 g** (26.96 − 26.32). **All** that oxygen
combines with hydrogen to form water — so the water contains 0.64 g of
oxygen. Since 0.72 g of water was collected, the mass of hydrogen in it
must be 0.72 − 0.64 = **0.08 g**. Now the familiar table:

|                        | H         | O         |
|------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| masses/g               | 0.08      | 0.64      |
| number of moles of atoms | 0.08/1  | 0.64/16   |
| number of moles        | 0.08      | 0.040     |
| ÷ smaller              | 2         | 1         |
| empirical formula      | **H₂O**   |           |

Two hydrogen atoms to every oxygen atom — the experiment lands on the
formula you have written since Chapter 1, but now you have *derived* it
from masses.

:::exam-hint
The whole experiment hinges on one conservation sentence worth quoting
in answers: **all the oxygen lost from the copper(II) oxide ends up in
the water**. That is why oxygen's share of the water is *read off the
dish* (0.64 g) and only hydrogen's must be *inferred* (0.72 − 0.64).
Questions love asking which mass comes from which measurement.
:::

:::misconception
"0.72 g of water means 0.72/18 = 0.04 mol of water, so we're done."
That shortcut uses the answer's formula — circular. The experiment's
point is to *derive* H₂O without assuming it: weigh the oxygen that
left the oxide (0.64 g), weigh the water formed (0.72 g), infer the
hydrogen (0.08 g), and let the mole table say 2 : 1. Only after the
table agrees with H₂O does the 18 g/mol check make sense as a
confirmation.
:::

sections.title: Working out formulae using percentage composition figures
sections.markdown:
The worked examples and practicals so far determined empirical formulae
**from masses**. In the exam you are often given **percentages by mass**
instead. The book's Example 5 shows the one extra step — and it is a
pleasant one.

**Example 5.** Find the empirical formula of a compound containing
**82.7% C** and **17.3% H** by mass (Aᵣ: H = 1, C = 12).

The percentage figures apply to **any amount you choose — so choose
100 g**. Then the percentages simply *become* masses: 82.7% of 100 g is
82.7 g. Table 5.1 does the rest:

|                                 | C         | H         |
|---------------------------------|-----------|-----------|
| percentages/%                   | 82.7      | 17.3      |
| masses in 100 g/g               | 82.7      | 17.3      |
| number of moles of atoms        | 82.7/12   | 17.3/1    |
| number of moles                 | 6.89      | 17.3      |
| ÷ smallest to get ratio         | 6.89/6.89 | 17.3/6.89 |
| ratio of moles                  | 1         | 2.5       |

The ratio comes out **1 : 2.5** — and here the book's HINT does the
exam-thinking for you. The empirical formula is the *whole-number* ratio,
so a fraction is not an error, it is a instruction to scale up: **multiply
both numbers by 2** to get **C₂H₅**, the empirical formula.

:::key-point
Percentages → assume 100 g → the percentages become masses → the
familiar table runs unchanged. The only new decision is at the ratio:
1 : 2.5 is not "rounded to" 1 : 2 or 1 : 3 — it is multiplied up to
whole numbers (2 : 5).
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's HINT draws the exact line between legitimate rounding and
corruption: calculating 17.3/6.89 gives **2.51** — rounding that to 2.5
(or 1.01 to 1) is fine; rounding 2.51 **to 3** is not. And a ratio like
1 : 1.33 is not rounded down to 1 : 1 — you multiply by 3 to obtain the
whole-number ratio. Halves ×2, thirds ×3, quarters ×4: recognise the
fraction, clear it honestly.
:::

:::misconception
"A ratio of 1 : 2.5 must be experimental error — round it to 1 : 2."
No: with correct data, 2.5 is telling you the simplest *whole-number*
ratio needs scaling. 1 : 2.5 → 2 : 5 → C₂H₅. Rounding a clean fraction
away instead of multiplying it up produces a formula that is not just
imprecise but chemically impossible to reconcile with the given
percentages.
:::

sections.title: Converting empirical formulae into molecular formulae
sections.markdown:
The C₂H₅ from the last section cannot be a real compound's formula — as
you will recognise once you meet organic chemistry in Unit 4. The
**[[molecular-formula]]** (the actual number of each atom present in a
molecule) has to be a **multiple** of the empirical formula, like C₄H₁₀.

The conversion needs exactly one extra piece of information: **the
relative formula mass of the compound** — or the mass of 1 mole, which is
just the Mᵣ in grams. The book continues the previous example: suppose
you are told the relative formula mass is **58**.

- Mᵣ of C₂H₅ = (2 × 12) + (5 × 1) = **29** (Aᵣ: H = 1, C = 12)
- How many times does 29 go into 58? **58 / 29 = 2**
- So the molecule contains **2 lots of C₂H₅**: the molecular formula is
  **C₄H₁₀**

That is the whole method: divide the given Mᵣ by the empirical-formula
Mᵣ, multiply the empirical formula by the answer. The ratio of elements
is untouched (both C and H scale by the same factor), which is why the
molecular formula always "cancels down" to the empirical formula.

:::key-point
Molecular formula = empirical formula × n, where
**n = Mᵣ(compound) ÷ Mᵣ(empirical formula)**. If n comes out as a
whole number, the data is consistent; if it does not, something upstream
(the percentage table or the Mᵣ) needs re-checking.
:::

:::exam-hint
Show the division as its own line (58 / 29 = 2) and *then* the scaled
formula — method marks live in the n step, not just the final C₄H₁₀.
And note what the book flags: knowing "a bit more organic chemistry"
(Unit 4) is how you'd *spot* that C₂H₅ is impossible — but you do not
need that knowledge in the exam; the Mᵣ does the deciding for you.
:::

:::misconception
"The molecular formula is C₂H₅ doubled in mass, so 2 × 29 = 58 —
therefore the molecular formula is 58." The Mᵣ is a number; the formula
is atoms. The factor n multiplies the **formula** (C₂H₅ → C₄H₁₀), not
the mass figure. Writing "the molecular formula is 2" or "is 58" confuses
the scaling factor with the formula itself.
:::

empirical-to-molecular conversion via Mᵣ. Book p. 62 questions → page
jump only (licensing law).

sections.title: Worked example 6 — and into the crucible: heating barium chloride crystals
sections.markdown:
**Example 6.** A compound has the empirical formula **CH₂**. If the
relative formula mass is **56**, work out the molecular formula.

- Mᵣ of CH₂ = 12 + (2 × 1) = **14**
- 56 / 14 = **4**
- The molecule contains 4 lots of CH₂: the molecular formula is **C₄H₈**

The book adds the closing check: the ratio of elements in the molecular
formula must be the same as in the empirical formula — and indeed
C₄H₈ cancels down to CH₂.

The section then turns the page to the crucible work that the next
sections calculate. Two REMINDERs from the book set the vocabulary: when
some substances crystallise from solution, water becomes chemically bound
to the salt — **water of crystallisation** — and the salt is said to be
**hydrated**; **[[anhydrous]]** means *without* water. Figure 5.15 shows
barium chloride crystals being heated in a crucible: the experiment that
will hand you the mass data for finding **n** in BaCl₂·nH₂O.

:::safety
Barium chloride is toxic, but a Bunsen flame is not hot enough to release
it into the atmosphere.
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's HINT asks the practical question you should be ready to
answer: **how can you be sure all the water has been driven off?** Heat
to **constant mass** — heat the crucible, weigh it, and repeat until the
mass remains constant. If the mass is still falling, water remains; when
it is constant, all the water has gone. The same constant-mass discipline
appeared in the metal-oxide practicals (section 20); it is the standard
answer wherever a crucible experiment is examined.
:::

:::misconception
"CH₂ with Mᵣ 56 must be C₂H₄ — because 2 × 14 = 28 and 28 is close to
56, so it 'rounds up'." n must be an exact division, not an
approximation: 56 / 14 = 4 exactly, giving C₄H₈. If your division does
not land on a whole number, the error is upstream (wrong Mᵣ or a
percentage-table slip) — never "round n to the nearest whole number and
hope".
:::

formula from empirical formula + Mᵣ. Book p. 62 questions → page jump
only (licensing law).
:::

sections.title: Interpreting symbols in equations in terms of moles
sections.markdown:
Take the methane equation you balanced in section 5:

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

Read at molecular level, it says 1 molecule of CH₄ combines with 2
molecules of O₂ to form 1 molecule of CO₂ and 2 molecules of H₂O. But
molecules are inconveniently small for calculation — and the mole fixes
that, because the same ratios hold for moles:

**1 mol CH₄ reacts with 2 mol O₂ to form 1 mol CO₂ and 2 mol H₂O**

Nothing about the equation's meaning has changed — "the ratios are still
the same", as the book puts it. The equation's big numbers do double
duty: they balance the atoms *and* they announce the proportions in
moles.

The book's KEY POINT pins the arithmetic: the big numbers in front of
the formulae tell us **the number of moles** of each substance that
react. And although there does not appear to be a big number in front of
the CH₄ and CO₂, there is — a '1' that we simply do not write.

:::key-point
A chemical equation can always be read as a mole recipe: the balancing
numbers are the moles. An invisible '1' counts as a big number
(CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ means 1 mol : 1 mol : 1 mol).
:::

:::exam-hint
This reading is the hinge between the first half of this chapter
(equations) and the second half (reacting masses): every mass calculation
from here on starts by *interpreting the equation in terms of moles*.
When a question says "using the equation", that instruction means: write
the mole row underneath the equation before touching any masses.
:::

:::misconception
"The equation means 1 *gram* of CH₄ reacts with 2 *grams* of O₂." No —
the balancing numbers are mole ratios, never gram ratios. In fact
1 mol CH₄ (16 g) reacts with 2 mol O₂ (64 g): the mass ratio is 16 : 64,
not 1 : 2. Grams and moles are connected through Mᵣ, which is exactly
why the next sections interpose a moles step between the equation and
the masses.
:::

as mole recipes. Book p. 62–63 questions → page jump only (licensing
law).
:::

sections.title: Empirical formula calculations involving water of crystallisation — finding n
sections.markdown:
Heat a salt that contains water of crystallisation and the water is
driven off, leaving the **[[anhydrous]]** salt behind. Barium chloride —
a **[[hydrated-salt]]** — is the commonly used example, because the
barium chloride itself does not decompose even on quite strong heating —
only the water leaves.

**The experiment** (heating the crystals in a crucible, Figure 5.15)
hands you three masses:

- mass of crucible = **30.00 g**
- mass of crucible + barium chloride crystals, BaCl₂·nH₂O = **32.44 g**
- mass of crucible + anhydrous barium chloride, BaCl₂ = **32.08 g**

**Finding n** means finding the ratio of the number of moles of BaCl₂ to
the number of moles of water — "it's just another empirical formula
calculation" (Aᵣ: H = 1, O = 16, Cl = 35.5, Ba = 137; Mᵣ of BaCl₂ = 137 +
2 × 35.5 = 208, Mᵣ of H₂O = 18):

- mass of BaCl₂ = 32.08 − 30.00 = **2.08 g**
- mass of water = 32.44 − 32.08 = **0.36 g**

Table 5.2:

|                       | BaCl₂       | H₂O       |
|-----------------------|-------------|-----------|
| masses/g              | 2.08        | 0.36      |
| ÷ Mᵣ for moles        | 2.08/208    | 0.36/18   |
| number of moles       | 0.0100      | 0.020     |
| ratio of moles        | 1           | 2         |
| empirical formula     | **BaCl₂·2H₂O** |        |

The unknown n was 2 — found by the identical divide-by-Mᵣ,
divide-by-smallest machinery as every other empirical formula in this
chapter. The only novelty is that one of the "elements" is a whole water
molecule.

:::exam-hint
Two Mᵣ values must be *assembled* before the table can start: BaCl₂ =
208 (137 + 2 × 35.5) and H₂O = 18. Show both constructions — the marks
sit in the assembly, and the table cannot misfire if 208 and 18 are
written explicitly. Note also which masses produce which subtraction:
crystals-minus-crucible gives the *hydrate*, anhydrous-minus-crucible
gives the *salt*, and their difference is the *water*.
:::

:::misconception
"n is found by dividing the mass of crystals by the mass of water." That
ignores the salt entirely: n is the ratio of **moles** — 0.020 mol water
to 0.010 mol BaCl₂ — not of masses (0.36/2.08 = 0.17 would be nonsense).
Convert each mass to moles with its own Mᵣ *first*; the ratio comes only
after both conversions.
:::

in hydrated salts. Book p. 62 questions → page jump only (licensing
law).

sections.title: Calculations using moles, chemical equations and masses of substances
sections.markdown:
Section 25 taught you to read an equation in moles. This section cashes
that in for **masses**. Take the methane equation again:

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

Interpreted in moles: **1 mol CH₄ reacts with 2 mol O₂** to form 1 mol
CO₂ and 2 mol H₂O. The book's KEY POINT adds the molecular bookkeeping
beneath it: 2 mol of O₂ contains twice as many molecules as 1 mol of
CH₄ — the proportions you weigh out are the proportions that the
molecules react in.

Now attach masses, using the Mᵣ values (CH₄ = 16, O₂ = 32, CO₂ = 44,
H₂O = 18):

- 1 mol CH₄ = **16 g** and 2 mol O₂ = **64 g** react exactly...
- ...to form 1 mol CO₂ = **44 g** and 2 mol H₂O = **36 g**

Check the bookkeeping with the conservation instinct from section 4:
16 + 64 = 80 g on the left; 44 + 36 = 80 g on the right. Mass conserved,
moles proportioned — the equation is now a quantitative recipe, and the
book's Figure 5.16 (glowing limestone) previews the first full problem
in the next section: limestone, impure calcium carbonate, decomposes on
heating to calcium oxide (quicklime) and carbon dioxide — a **thermal
decomposition** with Mᵣ(CaCO₃) = 100 and Mᵣ(CaO) = 56, the two numbers
you will need.

:::key-point
The mass scale of any reaction comes from its mole recipe: multiply each
mole count by the substance's mass of 1 mole. Conservation is the built-in
check — total mass of products must equal total mass of reactants.
:::

:::exam-hint
The four masses (16 g, 64 g, 44 g, 36 g) are worth deriving rather than
memorising: each is moles × Mᵣ, straight from the equation's big numbers.
Examiners ask this pattern constantly — "what mass of oxygen reacts with
16 g of methane?" — and the answer is always the same three moves:
equation → moles → mass.
:::

:::misconception
"If the equation says CH₄ + 2O₂, I need equal *masses* of methane and
oxygen." The equation proportions are moles (1 : 2), not grams. Converting
to masses gives 16 g : 64 g — oxygen's extra factor of 4 comes from its
Mᵣ being double methane's while you need double the moles. Confusing the
mole row with a mass row is the error that makes conservation look
broken.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.28/1.29 items — mole-recipe
to mass conversions. Book p. 62–63 questions → page jump only (licensing
law).
:::

sections.title: Calculations involving only masses
sections.markdown:
The reacting-mass problems are now in view, and the book describes the
exam's format precisely. Typical calculations give you a **mass of
starting material** and ask how much **product** you are likely to
obtain; you will also find them done **in reverse** — told the mass of
product, asked how much starting material you would need. And in almost
all the cases you will meet at International GCSE, **you will be given
the equation** for the reaction.

That last sentence is worth reading twice. The exam does not test
whether you can recall an equation mid-problem; it tests whether you can
*use* the one supplied — read it in moles (section 25), convert the given
mass to moles (section 16), walk the mole ratio, and convert back to
mass. The book's next sections run that pipeline through three complete
problems: heating calcium carbonate, extracting iron, and extracting
lead — each with the method spelled out and the alternative route shown.

The three-step skeleton those problems share:

1. **Calculate the number of moles** using the mass you have been given.
2. **Use the chemical equation** to work out the number of moles of the
   substance you are interested in.
3. **Convert the number of moles to a mass.**

:::exam-hint
"When you have finished a chemistry calculation, the impression should
nearly always be that there are a lot of words with a few numbers between
them, not vice versa" — the book's own description of a full-mark answer.
Show the equation-reading and the unit changes as words and lines, not as
a bare arithmetic stream: the words are where the method marks are parked.
:::

:::misconception
"Reacting-mass questions require memorising which equation belongs to
which reaction." At International GCSE, the equation is given in
almost all cases — the skill being tested is the moles pipeline, not
recall. Memorise the *pipeline* (mass → moles → ratio → moles → mass)
rather than reaction equations, and read the supplied equation carefully
for its balancing numbers.
:::

reacting-mass skeleton. Book p. 62–63 questions → page jump only
(licensing law).

sections.title: A problem involving heating calcium carbonate — the three-step method
sections.markdown:
When calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, is heated, calcium oxide is formed. The
task: **calculate the mass of calcium oxide produced by heating 25 g of
calcium carbonate** (Aᵣ: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40):

CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

**Step 1 — moles from the given mass.** Mᵣ(CaCO₃) = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) =
100, so:

number of moles = mass ÷ mass of 1 mole = 25 / 100 = **0.25 mol**

**Step 2 — the equation gives the target moles.** From the equation,
**1 mol of CaCO₃ decomposes to produce 1 mol of CaO** — so 0.25 mol
CaCO₃ produces **0.25 mol CaO**.

**Step 3 — moles back to mass.** Mᵣ(CaO) = 40 + 16 = 56:

mass = number of moles × mass of 1 mole = 0.25 × 56 = **14 g**

The reaction will produce **14 g of calcium oxide**.

**The alternative route (ratios).** The book's HINT shows the same answer
without the explicit moles: 1 mol CaCO₃ produces 1 mol CaO, so
100 g produces 56 g; therefore 1 g produces 56/100 = 0.56 g; therefore
25 g produces 25 × 0.56 = **14 g**. "You do not have to learn both
methods, just learn whichever method you are happier with."

Two more HINTs from the book complete the section. On precision: the
impression of a full-mark answer is "a lot of words with a few numbers
between them" — and even if your mental arithmetic is fast enough to
skip steps, **you must still show all your calculations**. On a
half-factor trap (which returns in the iron problem): to find the mass
of Fe you multiply moles of Fe by 56 — a common mistake is to multiply
by the mass of **2Fe** (112 g), but the '2' has *already been used* when
the moles of Fe were worked out from the equation.

:::key-point
The Aᵣ of Fe is 56; the Mᵣ of Fe₂O₃ = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160. These
are the two numbers the next problem runs on — assembled exactly as
here, from the Periodic Table values.
:::

:::exam-hint
The ratio method shines when the equation's coefficients are awkward or
the arithmetic is round-numbered (100 → 56 here). The three-step method
scales to *every* problem in the rest of the chapter, including the
two-equation lead problem where the ratio method gets messier. Learn one
primary method, keep the other as a checking tool — and remember the
book's warning to show the working either way.
:::

:::misconception
"CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ shows 3 substances, so 1 mol CaCO₃ gives 3 mol of
products." The big (or unwritten '1') numbers give **1 mol CaO and 1 mol
CO₂** separately — the mole row is read per substance, not summed into a
single "3". Step 2 needs the specific pair (CaCO₃ → CaO), which the
balancing numbers state directly.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.29 items — the three-step
method on thermal decomposition. Book p. 63 questions (including the
CaCO₃ family) → page jump only (licensing law).
:::

sections.title: A problem about extracting iron — a 2 : 1 mole ratio
sections.markdown:
The equation below is for a reaction that occurs in the extraction of
iron:

Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 2Fe + 3CO

**Calculate the mass of iron which can be formed from 1000 g of iron
oxide.**

**Step 1.** Mᵣ(Fe₂O₃) = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = **160** (the book's KEY
POINT builds it exactly so). So:

number of moles = 1000 / 160 = **6.25 mol Fe₂O₃**

**Step 2 — now the ratio matters.** From the equation, **1 mol Fe₂O₃
produces 2 mol Fe** — "we know this because of the big numbers in front
of the formulae". Starting with a certain number of moles of Fe₂O₃, you
obtain **twice as many** moles of Fe:

6.25 mol Fe₂O₃ → 2 × 6.25 = **12.5 mol Fe**

**Step 3.** Mass of 12.5 mol Fe = 12.5 × 56 = **700 g**.

**The alternative route (ratios):** 1 mol Fe₂O₃ produces 2 mol Fe, so
160 g (1 mol) of Fe₂O₃ produces 2 × 56 = 112 g (2 mol) of Fe; 1 g of
Fe₂O₃ produces 112/160 g; therefore 1000 g produces
1000 × 112/160 = **700 g**.

:::exam-hint
The book's HINTs arm you for industrial-scale variants: **you should be
told how many grams there are in a tonne** if the question needs it
(the conversion, Figure 5.18: 1 tonne = 1 000 000 g), and note that
1 000 000 might be written as 10⁶ or 1 × 10⁶ — "these are both the
same". The next section uses exactly this conversion.
:::

:::misconception
"1 mol Fe₂O₃ produces 1 mol Fe — the iron comes from the iron oxide, one
formula unit each." Read the equation: **2Fe**. Each Fe₂O₃ unit carries
*two* iron atoms, so each mole of it yields **two** moles of iron. The
balancing numbers encode the atom bookkeeping — 1 : 2 here — and
ignoring the 2 halves your answer (350 g instead of 700 g).
:::

Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.29 items — reacting-mass
problems with non-1:1 ratios. Book p. 63 questions → page jump only
(licensing law).
:::

sections.title: A problem involving the extraction of lead — two equations and a tonne
sections.markdown:
Lead is extracted from galena, PbS. The ore is roasted in air to produce
lead(II) oxide, PbO:

2PbS(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2PbO(s) + 2SO₂(g)

The lead(II) oxide is then converted to lead by heating it with carbon in
a blast furnace:

PbO(s) + C(s) → Pb(l) + CO(g)

The molten lead is tapped from the bottom of the furnace (Figure 5.17).
**Calculate the mass of lead that would be produced from 1 tonne of
galena.**

**Step 1 — mind the units.** Moles need grams, so convert: 1 tonne =
1 000 000 g (multiply by 1 000 000 — the number has to increase). Then,
with Mᵣ(PbS) = 207 + 32 = 239:

number of moles of PbS = 1 000 000 / 239 = **4184 mol**

**Step 2 — trace the lead through BOTH equations.** From the first:
2 mol PbS produce 2 mol PbO, so 4184 mol PbS → **4184 mol PbO**. From the
second: 1 mol PbO produces 1 mol Pb, so 4184 mol PbO → **4184 mol Pb**.

**Step 3 — back to mass, then to tonnes.** Mass of Pb = 4184 × 207 =
866 000 g. Divide by 1 000 000: **0.866 tonne** of lead.

The book's KEY POINT explains the doubling trick a second route uses:
double the second equation (2PbO + 2C → 2Pb + 2CO) so you can trace what
happens to **all** the 2PbO from the first — and then notes the
simplification: this could be reduced to *1 mol PbS produces 1 mol Pb*,
saving arithmetic, though it makes no difference to the answer. Its HINT
weighs the two methods: the three-step route uses the same steps in every
calculation but needs the tonne conversions; the ratio route has fewer
steps but will not extend to the solution calculations of the next
chapter.

:::cross-curricular
This flow sheet — roast the ore, reduce the oxide, tap the metal from
the furnace's base — is the extractive-metallurgy pattern that powered
the industrial revolution, and the blast furnace is still the reason
iron and lead (Chapter 14 revisits both) have been cheap enough to build
a metal-based civilisation on. The chemistry is old; the mole
arithmetic you just did is what makes the yields predictable.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two-equation problems are bookkeeping, not new chemistry: follow the
substance (here PbS → PbO → Pb) through each equation's own mole ratio,
in order. Write the mole row for each equation separately before
combining — and keep the tonne conversion at the very edges of the
problem (once in, once out), never in the middle of the mole arithmetic.
:::

:::misconception
"The two equations both start with 2, so 2 mol PbS gives 1 mol Pb."
Trace it: 2 mol PbS → 2 mol PbO (first equation), then 2 mol PbO → 2 mol
Pb (second). The lead count never halves — 2 mol PbS yields **2 mol Pb**.
The book's doubling of the second equation exists precisely to make this
chain visible; simplifying to 1 : 1 is a convenience, not a change.
:::

sections.title: What is a percentage yield?
sections.markdown:
If you calculate how much product a reaction *might* produce, in real
life you rarely obtain as much as you expected. Expect 100 g, collect
80 g — your percentage yield is **80%**. The rest is lost somehow, and
the book gives the standard loss mechanisms: **spillages**; losses when
transferring a liquid from one container to another; and — a big one —
**side reactions**, which divert some of your starting materials into
unwanted products. That, the book notes, "happens a lot during reactions
in organic chemistry" (its Figure 5.19 shows student experiments making
and purifying organic compounds, which rarely give high yields).

Percentage yield is also where the previous problem's arithmetic gets its
second life. Revisiting the lead calculation with the *ratios* route:
trace the lead through both equations — 2 mol PbS produces 2 mol PbO,
then (doubling the second equation) 2 mol PbO produces 2 mol Pb — so
every 2 mol of PbS produces 2 mol of Pb. Substitute masses: 2 × 239 g PbS
produces 2 × 207 g Pb, that is **478 g PbS produces 414 g Pb**. Tonnes
asked? "It's much easier to think a bit, and realise that the ratio is
always going to be the same, whatever the units": 478 tonnes PbS produces
414 tonnes Pb. Proportion: 1 tonne gives 414/478 = **0.866 tonne** — the
same answer as section 31, with no gram-conversion at all.

:::key-point
A proportion's ratio is unit-independent: 478 g : 414 g and
478 tonnes : 414 tonnes are the same 414/478. This is why the ratio
method can work directly in tonnes — the units cancel inside the
proportion.
:::

:::exam-hint
The "ratio is the same whatever the units" insight is a genuine exam
shortcut for any yield or reacting-mass question set in tonnes (or kg).
Use it *deliberately*: state the proportion in the question's own units,
then divide. It replaces the convert-in-convert-out arithmetic of the
three-step method — at the cost of the generality that method's HINT in
section 31 warned about.
:::

:::misconception
"A low percentage yield means I did the calculation wrong." No — the
calculated amount is the *theoretical* yield (what the equation promises);
the low percentage yield measures the *experiment's* losses against it.
Spills, transfer losses and side reactions are real chemistry, not
arithmetic errors. The next section defines the two yields formally and
does the division.
:::

short of theory. Book p. 63 questions → page jump only (licensing law).

sections.title: Calculating percentage yields
sections.markdown:
Suppose a calculation says you should get **12.5 g of copper sulfate
crystals**, but the experiment delivers only **11.2 g**. The book names
both numbers:

- **12.5 g is the [[theoretical-yield]]** — obtained by carrying out a
  moles calculation from the equation;
- **11.2 g is the [[actual-yield]]** — what the experiment actually
  produced, and it will be **given to you in the question**.

The formula is then one division:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Here: (11.2 / 12.5) × 100 = **89.6%**.

The book's HINT sets the sanity bound every marker looks for: **the
percentage yield should always come out as less than 100%**. If it comes
out above 100%, either you have made a mistake in the calculation, or the
question is deliberately continuing by asking what went wrong
experimentally. Its own example: if you are making a salt (Chapter 17),
a percentage yield above 100% can mean the salt **was not completely
dry** — extra water inflating the "product" mass.

:::key-point
Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100. The actual yield is
always the given number; the theoretical yield is always the one *you*
calculate from the equation. Never divide the other way.
:::

:::exam-hint
Identify which number is which before dividing — that is the entire
skill in this calculation type. Clues: the theoretical yield's context is
"calculate/could/might produce"; the actual yield's context is "she
made/obtained/collected". Worked example 7 (next section) shows the
theoretical yield being *derived* through a full two-equation mole
chain before the division — that derivation is where most of the marks
live.
:::

:::misconception
"A percentage yield of 89.6% means 10.4% of the atoms vanished."
Conservation of mass never breaks: the "missing" 10.4% of product is
unreacted starting material, product lost in transfers or purification,
or mass diverted into **side-reaction products** you did not count.
The yield measures how much of your product *ended up in the bottle*,
not whether atoms were destroyed.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 7 — percentage yield of copper(II) sulfate crystals
sections.markdown:
**Example 7.** A student reacted **2.40 g of copper(II) oxide (CuO)** with
hot sulfuric acid. She made **5.21 g of copper(II) sulfate crystals
(CuSO₄·5H₂O)**. The two reactions run in sequence: the copper(II) oxide
reacts with the sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate in solution, and
the copper(II) sulfate then crystallises from that solution with five
waters of crystallisation attached — CuSO₄ → CuSO₄·5H₂O, one formula unit
giving one formula unit of crystals. (In the printed book these two
equations appear as images; the stoichiometry is stated word-for-word in
the working that follows, and nothing here is invented.)

**Deriving the theoretical yield.** First, the moles of copper(II)
oxide — we have enough information to calculate them. Mᵣ(CuO) = 63.5 + 16
= 79.5:

number of moles of CuO = 2.40 / 79.5 = **0.0302 mol**

From the first reaction, **0.0302 mol CuO produces 0.0302 mol CuSO₄**
(one formula unit → one formula unit). From the crystallisation step,
**0.0302 mol CuSO₄ produces 0.0302 mol CuSO₄·5H₂O**.

Now convert to mass — the Mᵣ of the crystals is the one you built in
section 12: Mᵣ(CuSO₄·5H₂O) = **249.5**.

mass = 0.0302 × 249.5 = **7.53 g**

This is the **theoretical yield** of copper(II) sulfate crystals.

**The percentage yield.** The actual yield is what the experiment
obtained: **5.21 g**.

percentage yield = (5.21 / 7.53) × 100 = **69.2%**

:::key-point
A 1 : 1 : 1 mole chain (CuO → CuSO₄ → CuSO₄·5H₂O) means the *moles never
change* through the two steps — only the mass does, when each substance's
own Mᵣ is applied. The chain's job is to get you from the starting mass
to the theoretical yield of the *product as collected* (crystals
included).
:::

:::exam-hint
Two details make this example exam-hard. First, the product's Mᵣ must
include the **water of crystallisation** (249.5, not 159.5 for CuSO₄) —
use the wrong one and the whole calculation dies at the last step
(despite correct moles). Second, note the book's own number discipline:
0.0302 mol carries three significant figures because the mass data does.
The 69.2% then lands below 100% as it should (section 33's bound).
:::

:::misconception
"The theoretical yield is 2.40 g — the copper(II) oxide all becomes
product, so the masses match." The *moles* carry over 1 : 1, not the
masses: 0.0302 mol of CuO weighs 2.40 g, but the same 0.0302 mol of
CuSO₄·5H₂O weighs 0.0302 × 249.5 = 7.53 g — the sulfate and the five
waters add enormous mass. Each step multiplies by its own substance's
mass of 1 mole; only the mole count is conserved.
:::
