sections.title: Which substance is in excess?
sections.markdown:
When you make something in the lab, you rarely mix things in exactly the
right proportions. Usually **something is in excess** — there is more
than enough of it to react with the other substance — and you remove the
excess afterwards (by filtering, for example). A **[[reagent]]** is just
something that reacts; the substance left over is the
**[[excess-reagent]]**.

The trap the book sets up: until now, every problem gave you enough
information to calculate moles of **one** thing. What if you are given
moles of **both**?

> Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid:
> Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
> **0.2 mol Mg is reacted with 0.2 mol HCl. Calculate the mass of
> hydrogen gas produced.**

The tempting wrong answer: 0.2 mol Mg produces 0.2 mol H₂, so the mass of
H₂ = 0.2 × 2 = **0.4 g**. "Unfortunately this is not the correct answer!"
Check against the equation: 1 mol Mg reacts with **2 mol HCl**, so 0.2 mol
Mg would need **0.4 mol HCl** — but only 0.2 mol was used. The magnesium
cannot all react, so its moles cannot be used to work out the hydrogen.

Start from the HCl instead: 2 mol HCl reacts with 1 mol Mg, so 0.2 mol
HCl reacts with 0.1 mol Mg — and there *is* enough Mg (0.2 mol) to react
with all of it. **The Mg is in excess**, which means **all the HCl
reacts**, and HCl controls the product:

2 mol HCl produce 1 mol H₂ → 0.2 mol HCl produce **0.1 mol H₂**

mass of H₂ = 0.1 × 2 = **0.2 g** — the correct answer.

:::key-point
You **always have to use the chemical equation** to determine which
substance is in excess — "more of it" is not the test. The book's own
variant: 0.2 mol Mg with 0.3 mol HCl *looks* like HCl is in excess
(there is more of it), but 0.3 mol HCl only reacts with 0.15 mol Mg —
still not enough HCl to use up all the Mg, so the Mg is **still** in
excess.
:::

:::exam-hint
The book closes the method in one line: **to deduce which substance is
in excess, try both numbers of moles in the chemical equation and
compare**. Run each reagent's moles through the ratio and see which one
runs out first — the one that runs out (HCl here) is the limiting
reagent, and *it* — never the excess one — feeds the product
calculation.
:::

:::misconception
"Whichever reagent I have more moles of must be the one in excess."
Excess is a *ratio* property, not a size property: 0.3 mol of HCl against
0.2 mol of Mg still leaves HCl short, because the equation demands
2 mol HCl per 1 mol Mg. Always convert both amounts through the
equation's ratio before naming the excess.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 8 — excess with nitric acid, and the chapter close
sections.markdown:
**Example 8.** Copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid according to
the equation:

Cu(s) + 4HNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) + 2NO₂(g)

**3.2 g of copper** is reacted with **0.40 mol** of concentrated nitric
acid. Work out which reagent is in excess.

**Convert the copper mass to moles first** (Aᵣ: Cu = 63.5):

number of moles of Cu = 3.2 / 63.5 ≈ **0.050 mol**

**Run each reagent through the equation.** The equation says 1 mol Cu
reacts with **4 mol HNO₃**, so:

0.050 mol Cu reacts with 4 × 0.050 = **0.20 mol HNO₃**

We have **more** than 0.20 mol HNO₃ (we have 0.40 mol) — therefore
**HNO₃ is in excess** (and the copper is the limiting reagent).

The book's follow-through: if the question went further and asked for the
amount of NO₂ produced *using these quantities*, you would have to use
the **copper's** moles — not all the HNO₃ is used up. From the equation,
2 mol Cu produce 2 mol NO₂, so 0.050 mol Cu gives 2 × 0.050 =
**0.10 mol NO₂**. This is exactly the section 35 law: the limiting
reagent feeds the product calculation.

The chapter's question set (pp. 60–63) then drills everything: balancing
equations, mole and molar-mass conversions, empirical formulae from
percentages, reacting masses through CaCO₃ and the extraction reactions,
and yield problems — **page jump only** (licensing law: the questions
stay in the book; this lesson's practice is wired to the question bank
through the derived-links quick-checks above).

:::summary
- Equations must **balance** — same atoms out as in. Balance with big
  numbers only; **never change a formula**. State symbols: (s), (l),
  (g), (aq).
- Big numbers = coefficients = **moles**; subscripts belong to the atom
  (or bracket) before them (2H₂SO₄ = 4 H, 2 S, 8 O).
- **Mᵣ** = sum of the Aᵣ values (hydrated salts include their waters:
  CuSO₄·5H₂O = 159.5 + 90 = 249.5); **mass of 1 mole = Mᵣ in grams**.
- **1 mol = 6 × 10²³ particles** (the Avogadro constant); moles =
  mass ÷ mass of 1 mole.
- **Empirical formula** = simplest whole-number ratio (from masses or
  percentages → assume 100 g); **molecular formula** = empirical × n,
  n = Mᵣ(compound) ÷ Mᵣ(empirical).
- Formulae *from experiments*: metal oxides by combustion or reduction
  (spec 1.36); water from collected masses; n in BaCl₂·nH₂O.
- Reacting masses: **mass → moles → equation ratio → moles → mass**.
  The limiting reagent (never the excess one) feeds the product.
- **Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100** — always < 100%
  unless something went wrong (or the product is wet).
:::

      (2H₂SO₄; Ca(OH)₂)?

:::exam-hint
One chapter, one spine: **the mole converts between what you can weigh
(grams) and what actually reacts (particles)**. Every exam question in
this chapter is that conversion wearing a different coat — equation
reading, Mᵣ assembly, empirical formulae, practicals, yields, excess.
When a question looks unfamiliar, find which link of the chain it is
testing and run that link; the book's question set (pp. 60–63) maps the
coats one-to-one.
:::

"This chapter is eight separate skills to memorise." It is one skill —
mole bookkeeping — applied eight ways. The HINT from section 28 says the
deep version: a full-mark answer is "a lot of words with a few numbers
between them". If you can *say* which link each calculation runs
through, the numbers follow; if you cannot say it, no formula-triangle
will save the answer.
:::
